The storm had knocked out the power in Ujjain, and Sarita's phone was on four percent when the message from the groom's aunt came through.
"No demands at all, beta, you know us. Just the usual custom: a fridge, a double bed, gold set for the bride, and a car for the boy, whatever you like. Engagement is tomorrow, so confirm tonight."
Sarita read it out by candlelight. Her mother's face went grey. "Custom," her mother repeated. "Everyone gives."
Her brother Vaibhav took the phone and scrolled. "Ma, this is a list. A list with a deadline. If they'd truly asked nothing, there'd be nothing to confirm. This is dowry, and it's against the law."
The phone died in his hand. In the dark, nobody spoke.
Then Sarita said, "Charge it at the neighbour's. Before the engagement, I'm calling him myself and asking whether he knows about this list."

qa.q: What did the groom's aunt ask the family to do tonight?
qa.a: The aunt asked them to confirm tonight, because the engagement is tomorrow.

qa.q: What was Sarita's mother feeling when her face went grey?
qa.a: She felt shocked and afraid, and tried to calm herself by repeating that it was custom and everyone gives.

qa.q: Why was Vaibhav right to call the message a list?
qa.a: It named specific items and set a deadline, so despite the words "no demands" it was an expectation, which is dowry; naming it clearly is the first step to refusing it.

qa.q: How might the groom feel when Sarita calls to ask about the list?
qa.a: If he did not know, he might feel embarrassed and angry at his aunt; if he did, Sarita's direct question forces him to face the demand openly.

grounding: It shows a bride's family told there are no demands, only custom, while receiving a list of items, and recognising it as dowry.

At the lunch meeting in the hotel in Chembur, the groom's father spread his hands. "We don't want anything, Rekha-ji. Nothing at all. Only, our relatives expect the wedding at a good venue. Five hundred guests. Silver gifts for each family. And of course, whatever you give your daughter is hers."
Rekha smiled politely and kept stirring her tea long after the sugar had dissolved.
Ira, twenty-four, the bride, sat beside her mother and did the sums in her head. The venue alone would swallow her parents' savings. Silver for every family. Gold "for her" that she knew would be counted.
On the taxi ride home, Ira said, "Mumma, they said 'nothing' and then listed four things."
Rekha stared out of the window. "It's how it's done."
"Then we need to decide if it's how we do it," Ira said. "I'd rather have a small wedding than start by paying for respect."

qa.a: He mentioned five hundred guests.

qa.q: What does Rekha stirring her tea long after the sugar had dissolved suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Rekha felt uneasy and trapped, keeping a polite smile while she worried about expectations she could not easily meet.

qa.q: What could Ira and Rekha do next?
qa.a: They could talk as a family about what they will and won't provide, and then tell the groom's side calmly and early, perhaps with a trusted elder present, that they want a simple wedding.

qa.a: Rekha accepts them as how things are done, but Ira hears the list hidden in "nothing" and sees it as dowry dressed as custom.

Supervisor's note, accounts office, 12 November.
Uma, 26, one of our steadiest staff, asked me for a large salary advance today, the second this year. When I asked gently what it was for, she said it was for her younger sister's wedding. The groom's family had asked for a car "as a token of love," and her father, Bhupen, had already borrowed from two relatives.
Uma said, "If we don't give it, they'll treat my sister badly after the wedding. Papa is scared. I'm scared."
She looked exhausted. I did not lecture her. I told her that what she described sounded like dowry, and that her fear made sense. I gave her the number of the women's helpline and of the family counselling centre near the office. She said she would call the helpline with her father this evening. I have not approved the advance yet and will check in with her tomorrow.

qa.a: The groom's family had asked for a car "as a token of love."

qa.a: Uma is afraid that if the family does not give the car, her sister will be treated badly after the wedding; she and her father are both scared.

qa.a: The supervisor listened without lecturing, said her fear made sense, named what she described as dowry and gave her the helpline and counselling numbers, then planned to check in the next day.

The women's help desk at the district hospital had pale green walls and a fan that clicked on every turn. Zeenat sat on the bench with her dupatta pulled low.
When her turn came, the counsellor, Hafsa, offered her water and waited.
"It's not beating," Zeenat said at last. "It's words. Every day. My mother-in-law says my family sent cheap things. Now my husband wants money for a shop, and he says my father should pay it since he gave so little."
"How long?"
"Since the wedding. Eight months."
Hafsa didn't look shocked. "What you're describing has a name. Repeated demands for money after marriage, and taunts about what your family gave, are harassment. It isn't custom, and it isn't your fault."
Zeenat's shoulders dropped. Hafsa wrote down a legal-aid number and asked, "Is there someone in your family you trust? Can we call them now, together?"

qa.q: How long have the taunts been going on?
qa.a: Since the wedding, for eight months.

qa.q: What does Zeenat's shoulders dropping suggest she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt relieved and less alone when Hafsa said it was harassment, not custom, and not her fault.

qa.q: What made Hafsa's response helpful?
qa.a: Hafsa listened calmly, named the demands as harassment, told Zeenat it wasn't her fault, gave a legal-aid number and offered to call a trusted family member together right then.

You asked me, Vaibhav, why I volunteer at the helpline. So here it is.
The first year of my marriage, my father-in-law kept a notebook. I'm serious. He wrote down every gift my family had given, and every festival he'd add a line of what was "still pending." A TV. A scooter. At dinner he'd read it out, laughing, like a joke.

I was there when Charu spoke up, so I can tell you exactly how it went, though not what was going on inside her.
It was the first planning meeting for my sister's wedding. Our aunts were making a list for the groom's family: clothes, utensils, a sofa set. Charu, our cousin, had been quiet all morning. Class teacher's note, Class 4B, Thursday.
In art today I asked the children to draw "My Sunday." Disha drew herself at the sink, a pile of plates, and a boy outside with a kite. When I asked who the boy was, she said, "My brother. He gets to fly kites. I help Mummy." She said it plainly, without complaint, but she coloured the kite very carefully, three times over.
I did not comment in class. After school I rang her mother, Tanuja, and told her about the drawing, only what I had seen. Tanuja was quiet, then said, "I never noticed. I did the same at her age." She said she would ask Disha's brother to share the dishes this weekend and let Disha fly the kite too.

qa.q: What small step did the teacher take, and why was it wise?
qa.a: The teacher told Tanuja privately and only described the drawing, which let Tanuja notice the pattern herself without shaming Disha or the family.

Dear Diary,
Today after school Amma called me to roll chapatis. Mohit was watching cartoons. I asked, "Why not Mohit?" Amma said, "He's a boy, Gopika. Boys don't roll."
I rolled eleven chapatis. Some were not round. Mohit came and ate three and said mine looked like maps.
I was angry but I didn't know why exactly. It's just chapatis.
At night Appa came home and saw me rubbing my arm. He asked why. I told him. Appa said, "Mohit, tomorrow you roll, and Gopika watches cartoons." Mohit made a face.
Then Appa said he would roll too! His chapati looked like a map of Africa. We laughed so much.
I think tomorrow will be fair.
Gopika

qa.a: Gopika rolled eleven chapatis.

qa.a: Gopika felt angry, though she didn't know exactly why, because Mohit watched cartoons while she worked.

qa.a: Appa asked Mohit to roll the next day and rolled chapatis himself, showing that cooking is for everyone.

qa.a: Gopika might keep rolling every day while Mohit played, and both children would learn that chores depend on being a girl or a boy.

In their kasba, the last bus from the tuition centre came at 6:30. Sunaina, fifteen, had to take it, because Papa said girls should be home before the lamps were lit. Her brother cycled back from cricket at 8 whenever he liked.
One evening the bus broke down and Sunaina walked the last stretch, heart thumping, as it got dark. When she reached home, Papa was pacing at the gate. He shouted, then hugged her hard.
That night, Lavanya Aunty from next door, a nurse, came over. She said, "The road by the canal has no lights. That's the real danger, for any child." She suggested Sunaina and her brother both come home by the lit main road, and together if one was late.
Papa looked at Sunaina's brother. "Both of you. Same rule." Sunaina felt her shoulders loosen.

qa.q: When did the last bus from the tuition centre come?
qa.a: The last bus from the tuition centre came at 6:30.

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel when Papa set the same rule for both?
qa.a: Sunaina felt relieved, her shoulders loosening, because the rule finally felt fair rather than aimed only at her.

qa.q: What made Lavanya Aunty's suggestion useful?
qa.a: She named the real risk, the unlit canal road, and suggested a rule that applied to any child, which made the family's plan both safer and fairer.

qa.q: How did Papa seem to feel when Sunaina arrived late?
qa.a: Papa was frightened and relieved at once; he paced, shouted, then hugged her hard, which shows his rules came from fear for her.

grounding: In a small town, a teenage girl must be home before dark while her brother moves freely, and an honest talk about real risks leads to a fair shared rule.

passage:
The calf died on a Tuesday morning, and Suraj, fourteen, found her in the shed. He had fed her by hand since she was born.
He sat in the straw and cried until his chest hurt. His uncle came to the door. "Arre, a boy crying over a calf? Be strong. Get up."
Suraj wiped his face fast and laughed too loudly. "Just dust in my eyes, Chacha." At school he joked about it all day.
That evening his elder sister Gargi found him behind the well, kicking stones. She sat down next to him. "You loved her. It's okay to be sad."
Suraj stopped kicking. Then he cried again, and Gargi let him. Later, she told their mother what Chacha had said, and their mother told Chacha firmly, "Let the boy grieve."

qa.q: Who found the calf in the shed?
qa.a: Suraj, fourteen, found her in the shed.

qa.q: Why did Suraj laugh too loudly and joke all day?
qa.a: Suraj was hiding his grief and shame after his uncle told him to be strong, covering sadness with jokes.

qa.q: How did Gargi and their mother help Suraj?
qa.a: Gargi sat with him and said it was okay to be sad, and their mother told Chacha firmly to let him grieve, protecting his honesty about his feelings.

qa.q: How might Chacha's words affect Suraj in the future?
qa.a: If nobody had stepped in, Suraj might keep learning that boys must hide sadness behind jokes or anger.

grounding: A boy is told to be strong and stop crying, hides grief behind jokes and anger, and family members protect his right to feel sad.

After Lars missed the penalty in the under-16 final in Gothenburg, he sat on the bench with his hands over his face. His shoulders were shaking.
"Stop crying, Lars," one of the fathers called from the stands. "Be a man about it."
Lars dropped his hands and grinned. "Guess I'll be a goalkeeper," he joked. His teammate Kwame didn't laugh. For the next week Lars laughed at everything and snapped at anyone who mentioned the match.
On Friday, the coach asked Lars and Kwame to stay behind. "I cried after I lost my first final," the coach said. "It meant I cared. Nobody gets to take that from you."
Lars stared at his boots for a long time. Then he said, "It felt like I let everyone down."
Kwame nudged him. "You didn't. You were brave enough to take it."

qa.a: The under-16 final was in Gothenburg.

qa.q: Why did Lars joke and snap at people all week?
qa.a: He was hiding his sadness and shame after being told to be a man, so he covered it with jokes and irritation.

qa.q: What did the coach do that helped Lars?
qa.a: The coach shared a personal story and said crying meant caring, which made it safe for Lars to say he felt he let everyone down.

qa.q: How might Kwame see Lars's jokes?
qa.a: Kwame doesn't laugh, so he probably sees the jokes as a cover for how hurt Lars really is, and he wants to reassure him.

grounding: Outside India, a boy is told to stop crying, hides sadness behind jokes and anger, and an adult protects his emotional honesty.

In the boys' hostel at the residential school, the rule was simple: nobody cried where anyone could see. Abhinav, fifteen, learned it in his first week, when a senior mocked a boy who missed home.
So when his grandfather died in March, Abhinav punched the washroom door instead. He picked a fight at football. He told jokes at dinner until even his friends went quiet.
The warden, Chaitanya Sir, called him to the office the next evening. He didn't ask about the fight first. He said, "I heard about your grandfather. I'm sorry."
Abhinav's jaw worked. "I'm fine, sir."
"You don't have to be fine here," Chaitanya Sir said quietly, and shut the door.
Abhinav cried for twenty minutes. Chaitanya Sir waited, then called his mother so they could talk, and arranged for him to see the school counsellor the next morning.

qa.q: Who called Abhinav to the office?
qa.a: The warden, Chaitanya Sir, called him to the office.

qa.q: What does Abhinav punching the washroom door suggest he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt deep grief and anger, but couldn't show sadness openly because of the hostel's rule.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya Sir do well?
qa.a: He began with the grandfather's death rather than the fight, said Abhinav didn't have to be fine, waited while he cried, then called his mother and arranged a counsellor visit.

qa.q: How might Abhinav's friends feel when he tells jokes until they go quiet?
qa.a: They may feel uneasy and worried, sensing that the jokes are covering something painful.

grounding: In a hostel, a boy who has learned not to cry hides grief behind anger and jokes, and an adult protects his emotional honesty.

Pradeep, you know me as the guy who quit engineering. Here's what really happened.
Everyone in my family said the same thing: "You're the son. You have to earn well." My cousin sister was told to take a bank job, simple and safe, because she'd marry. Nobody asked either of us what we liked.
I liked caring for people. When Nani was in hospital, I stayed three nights and the nurses said I had steady hands. I wanted to be a nurse. I said it once at dinner and my uncle laughed so hard he coughed.
